Completing a garden costs `target − current`, which is smallest for the biggest gardens. And the minimum of the remaining gardens (the partial score) is raised by having the LOWEST gardens as the remaining ones. So completed gardens are always a suffix of the sorted order; trying every suffix length `k` and optimising the rest by binary search finds the best split.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Keep reducing until the string has at most `k` characters
Repeat a transformation until a condition is met
Start indices of consecutive groups of size `k` (the last one may be shorter)
One group (slices past the end are safe)
Concatenate the group sums into the next string

blocks.p: Each group of `k` digits is replaced by the decimal form of its digit sum. That sum is at most `9k`, which never has more digits than the group (for example `99` becomes `18`, still two digits, while a group of three digits has a sum below 28). So the string never grows, and it shrinks quickly once `k` is 3 or more, until its length is at most `k`.

bullets: Time: O(n) per round, with the length shrinking geometrically, so O(n) overall.

2243.takeaway: Digit sum of a string: repeatedly split into groups of k, replace each group by its digit sum, until the length is at most k.

p: `parent = [-1,0,0,1,1,2]`, `s = "abacbe"` (post-order):

The best path through `u` may use two child branches, but a path continuing upward can use only one. So we record `top1 + top2 + 1` in the global best and return only `top1 + 1`. This is the same pattern as Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum and Diameter of a Binary Tree.

2246.takeaway: Longest path with different adjacent characters: tree DP keeping the two best child branches; update the global best with their sum and return only the best one.

blocks.h: Why the extra slack at the safehouse?

`while st and st[-1] < h: st.pop(); ans += 1`
Each shorter person is visible (nobody between blocks them), and they are hidden from everyone further left by `h`
Count and remove the people that `h` hides

p: Row `[3,1,4,2,5]`, scanning from the right (only the row pass is shown):
The counts for the row are `[2,1,2,1,0]`: the person of height 3 sees the 1 and the 4 (and then is blocked); the person of height 5 at the end sees nobody.

blocks.h: Why must equal heights be skipped?
p: A person of height 4 can see a person of height 4 to the right (the problem says the person between must be shorter than both) but not beyond them. Pushing duplicates would let a later person count the farther equal-height person as visible. Keeping only one copy preserves the strict ordering.

head: Approach

rows: monotonic stack per row and column (this code)

bullets: Space: O(m·n) for the answer, O(max(m, n)) for the stack.

2282.takeaway: People visible in a grid: a monotonic stack scanned from the right (rows) and from the bottom (columns); popped shorter people plus one blocker are counted.

blocks.h: Why a ceiling and not `success / s`?
p: Potion strengths are integers. For a spell of 3, a potion of 2 gives 6 (< 7) and a potion of 3 gives 9 (≥ 7), so the threshold is `ceil(7/3) = 3`. Floor division would give 2 and wrongly count potion 2.
